title: Never the Star
text: The nautilus was never the star of the prehistoric ocean. It lived on the margins, ate scraps, and grew slowly.
nxt: And that may be exactly why it survived the asteroid.

title: The Twilight Zone
text: Today, it lives along the steep slopes of coral reefs, in the dim twilight zone, roughly two hundred to seven hundred meters down.
nxt: Many ammonites are thought to have lived in the sunlit upper ocean.

title: A Scavenger
text: The nautilus has strong, beak-like jaws, and its pinhole eyes have no lens, so it sees only a blurry picture.
nxt: It uses up to about ninety tentacles to sense chemicals in the water and find food, such as dead animals and shed crustacean shells.

title: Slow Metabolism
text: It also has a very low metabolic rate, and it can go a long time without eating.
nxt: Ammonites probably lived faster lives in bright, food-rich water, which would have meant a steady need for fresh food.

title: Lights Out
text: When the asteroid hit, dust, soot, and sulfur-rich particles blocked much of the sunlight for months,
nxt: perhaps years, and made the planet colder.

title: Waiting It Out
text: When that rain of food ended, its slow metabolism let it survive long periods with little to eat,
nxt: far longer than an animal that burns energy quickly. Waiting out hard times was exactly what the nautilus was built to do.

title: Still Here
text: Even so, the nautilus came through narrowly. Today only a handful of species remain, and they are caught for their shells.
nxt: In 2017, all nautiluses were listed under CITES Appendix II. The full story is on Miya's Lab.
